- The ACT Hexagon: A Model for Increasing Psychological Flexibility (Hexaflex Model): Kind: captions Language: en Acceptance and Commitment Therapy is built on empirically based principles aimed to increase psychological flexibility using a mindfulness-based approach with behavior change strategies. We’ve said that several times in this training and it bears repeating. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy is built on functional contextualism and relational frame theory and aims to increase psychological flexibility while using mindfulness interventions during empirically supported treatment plans. There are many different ways to discuss ACT. And one traditional introductory approach to the therapy is to use the ACT hexagon model. Steve Hayes and fellow behavioral scientists developed this six-point approach to discuss the components that lead clients to greater psychological flexibility. The ACT community embraces the idea that Acceptance and Commitment Therapy establishes greater psychological flexibility primarily through acceptance, defusion, establishment of a transcendent sense of self otherwise known as the self as context, contact with the present moment, values and building larger and larger patterns of committed action linked to those values. These six components form the ACT hexagon model which is sometimes humorously referred to as the hexaflex model because it is the hexagon that leads to flexibility. Please take a look at this conventional ACT hexagon model. And keep in mind that ACT comes from the foundation of behavior analysis and resides in the realm of cognitive behavioral therapy. Both behavior analysis and cognitive behavioral therapy are traditionally linear in their basic models. For instance, behavior analysis provided the historical context for ACT and the typical behavior analyst takes a look at the study of behavior through an ABC model. Traditional behavior analysts talk about the antecedent-behavior-consequence functions. A is followed by B which is followed by C. Antecedents set the occasion for behavior to occur. And after the behavior, a consequence will make it more or less likely for that behavior to happen again. This is a linear process. And if you look at traditional CBT models, they are often linear models as well. For instance, Albert Ellis, one of the chief pioneers of CBT, the developer of Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy, forwarded an ABC model as well. REBT assumes that there are activating events that elicit beliefs that are followed by emotional consequences. If something happens in the environment that is aversive, it can be an activating event that leads to an irrational belief which can lead to clinically relevant emotional consequences. In REBT treatment, this is to be followed by disputation in order to lead to effective emotion and action. So this is actually an ABCDE model. Again, very linear. And Acceptance and Commitment Therapy comes from both traditional behavior analysis and is part of the CBT community. But look at the ACT model. It isn’t a linear model. It is a circular model. You can joke around with me and say, it isn’t a circular model. It’s a hexagonal model. And I’d laugh and have to agree. But in Philosophy, when we talk about circular models, we’re highlighting that a method doesn’t have a specific beginning point or ending point. And let’s highlight that all the points on this model are equidistant from the center. So none of the components are more important than the other ones. The reason I’m highlighting this idea is not just to make an academic point about the history of ACT or to make a philosophical point about the model but to emphasize two important application ideas. One is that as you start to do the therapy, you will not likely access treatment plans or develop treatment plans that say, in session one, we’ll talk about defusion and in session two, we’ll cover values and in session three, we’ll talk about self as context and so on. Could you imagine trying to help a client build psychological flexibility with such a rigid and inflexible treatment plan? In ACT, the therapist is going to model the In other words, you as the clinician will perform ACT more effectively if you observe your client’s clinically relevant concerns as they show up in the therapy room and then flexibly move through the model to address whatever is showing up in the present moment. You flexibly model the model of flexibility. I mentioned that there are two important application ideas. The second idea is that being able to effectively model flexibility will require your own mindfulness skills. If you are going to effectively respond to your client, it will help a great deal if you work on contacting the present moment as regularly and fluidly as possible. You will once again be called on to model the model. Clients may regularly bring up new topics and issues that contribute to their own psychological inflexibility. It is incumbent on the therapist to be in the here and now. Focus on the client’s verbal behavior and overt behavior and then address any clinical issues that come up with one of the points on the hexagon model. You mindfully model the model of mindfulness. It will be helpful for the client to see your commitment to flexibility and mindfulness. Each one of these ACT components, acceptance, defusion, self as context, contact with the present moment, values and committed action, each one of them have their own way of being measured and each of them have different interventions and skills building exercises. And this is a situation where the whole is greater than the sum of the parts. ACT utilizes these six components to blend together and increase psychological flexibility for the client. And if you recall from a previous video, the more psychologically flexible you are, the lower your scores are on measures of psychopathology and the higher your scores are on quality of life inventories. We’ll walk through each one of these six components in the next two modules. But before we do a deeper dive into the details of the ACT hexagon model, it is important to highlight several ideas that have yet to be mentioned. First, the ACT hexagon model is not the only way of talking about Acceptance and Commitment Therapy. There are other approaches such as the mindful action plan, the choice point, the DNA-v model and the ACT matrix just to name a few. So as you continue to explore Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, you will see it is a robust therapeutic endeavor with diverse ways of leading to psychological flexibility. ACT embraces solid clinical skills Empathy Self-compassion Collaborative stance Self-disclosure Second, ACT embraces solid clinical skills in order to assist clients in developing We will not spend too much time on these concepts in this training but understand that there is an assumption that clinicians will have empathy for their clients, teach concepts like self-compassion and show unconditional positive regard with an equal collaborative stance rather than an authoritative stance. The therapist will meet the client where they are at and not force the hexagon exercises on the client in some kind of problematic manner. Self-disclosure might also be a part of the therapy if the clinician is ready for such a therapy move. We would want to demonstrate in session the oft used phrase in the ACT community that we all swim in the same soup. or in other words, every person needs help dealing with the human condition which leads to the third point. It will be very helpful if you, the consumer of this training, could start to embrace these concepts and apply them to your own issues. A psychologically flexible therapist is likely to be more effective not just through modeling the approach but in actually executing the applications with the client as well. In modules 2 and 3, we will introduce the six essential components from the ACT hexagon and bring them all together to show how they facilitate each other in order to accelerate psychological flexibility. I thank you very much for completing module 1 of the Demystifying ACT. Before moving to module 2 or prior to taking a break between trainings, I’m going to invite you to center yourself with a closing mindfulness exercise. Take a nice clean full breath. And if it is safe to do so during your next exhale, close your eyes. And for the next few moments, I’ll ask you to stay committed to attending to your breath. Notice what it feels like to inhale and exhale. Notice the rise and fall of your chest, the coolness of the air as you inhale and how it is warmer when you exhale. And if any thoughts come up that distract you from such a simple present focused commitment, I’ll simply ask you to gently bring your attention back to the invitation to attend to what you are doing in this present moment. Breathing. And I will invite you to take this same approach to any other behaviors you do after this training is over. Invite yourself to be fully in the present moment committed to your important actions and simply aware of but not distracted by any thoughts or emotions you’re experiencing. And now, I will invite you to take another full clean deep breath. And when you exhale, open your eyes and prepare to be psychologically flexible as you go about your day. There are 3 key points in this video. 1. There are many different ways to discuss Acceptance and Commitment Therapy but this training will focus on the traditional introductory approach using the ACT hexagon model. 2. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy’s hexagon model is non-linear, meaning that it is used flexibly depending upon what is showing up in the room with the client’s clinically relevant concern and such fluid usage will benefit from the clinician being more mindful of the present moment themselves. 3. ACT is applied within the framework of good solid therapeutic relationships. And therefore, what you do as a therapist as long as it is effective is likely to blend very well with the Acceptance and Commitment Therapy model.

- Defusion: How to Detangle from Thoughts & Feelings: Kind: captions Language: en-US Do you ever feel as if your thoughts dictate how your day goes? Or how you interact with others? Does it sometimes feel exhausting trying to shut your thoughts off? In today's video, I'm going to teach you a skill called defusion and this skill will help you get some distance from unhelpful thoughts, from unhelpful beliefs, emotions, images, and other inner experiences. Be mindful that throughout this video I'll use the word "thought" or "thoughts" to capture all these inner experiences that i kind of just mentioned. Defusion is a skill that is perfect for anyone who struggles with recurrent "negative" thoughts, or thoughts that significantly impact mood and behavior. It's also quite helpful for those who struggle with depressive and anxiety symptoms and, quite frankly, is pretty useful for anyone because, let's be honest, we all kind of get caught up and tangled with our thoughts and emotions from time-to-time. So, let me introduce myself. I am Dr. Gabriela Sadurní Rodríguez, licensed psychologist here at The Psychology Group. And without further adieu, let's begin First, let me explain a little bit about defusion before getting into the technique itself. Defusion is a skill that is primarily used to detach, separate, or get some distance from our thoughts and emotions. (All the inner experiences) And defusion is part of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy or ACT. ACT actually poses an interesting idea for thoughts; instead of trying to change, fight, or repress our inner experiences like thoughts, emotions, memories, sensations and all of this... we can focus on changing how we relate with them. Our minds tell us different stories because that's just what minds do. In the ACT framework, the content of the thought is not a problem, it's how we relate to it that can create the problem itself. So, for example, if you have the thought, "I am useless," and are completely fused with it by giving it your full attention, believing it, getting caught up in it, then you might feel sad or bad about yourself and avoid doing things that are important and or meaningful to you. When we are fused with our thoughts, we might believe them as a hundred percent true. And thus, thoughts could dictate our behavior. Believing thoughts such as, "I am useless," is probably not helpful and could affect every aspect of your life. Understanding this concept is important when learning about diffusion. According to Russ Harris, writer of ACT Made Simple, cognitive defusion is: looking at thoughts rather than from thoughts. Noticing rather than becoming caught up in them. Letting thoughts come and go rather than holding on to them. The aim of defusion is to: decrease our attachment to our inner experiences. Reduce the believability of thoughts. Decrease the influence of thoughts on our behaviors and experiences. Increase our ability to be present and take effective action. And most importantly, facilitate psychological flexibility. With defusion techniques you do not battle difficult thoughts, instead, you choose how much attention you pay to them. It also helps to ask yourself: is holding on to this thought or belief helpful? Is doing so causing me suffering or keeping me from being effective? Am I being pushed around by my thoughts? These questions aid in better understanding the workability concept. The workability concept is assessing if what we're doing is working to live a meaningful life. It's also choosing to take action based on what works instead of what is true. Okay, now that you have a better understanding of the importance of our relationship with our thoughts, let's get into an experiential example to better understand these concepts and the skill. So, I'm going to be walking you through the "Hands as Thoughts" metaphor, and this is by the same author I mentioned, Russ Harris, and the same book, ACT Made Simple. So, we try to adapt it a little bit for here... So, feel free to follow along if you like. First, I want you to put your hands together, palms facing upwards, as if they were pages of an open book. And I want you to start to imagine that your hands are your thoughts. And now, slowly, raise your hands up towards your face until you are covering your eyes and you can only see through the gaps of your fingers. Take a look around and notice how this impacts your view and your connection with your environment. How does it feel? Notice it is quite difficult to see much other than your hands and in this case, your thoughts. So, what would it be like to go around your day this way? Would you be limited or miss out on things? Would it be challenging to respond to others or the world around you? Chances are that you're answering "yes" to all these questions. Of course it is. This is a good representation of fusion. We become so entangled with our thoughts that we get disconnected from an environment and the here and now experience. Similarly, our thoughts also have a big impact on our behavior and our capacity to be effective. Now, slowly begin lowering your hands... and start noticing the difference. How does it feel? Can you notice that as the distance between your hands (your thoughts) and your eyes increase you're able to take in much more information and it's easier to connect with others and the environment? This is a good representation of defusion. Notice that your hands (your thoughts) are still there, they did not magically disappear, and that you can now look at them without becoming entangled with them. So, basically, if the thoughts are useful or workable to you you may use them. And if they are not then you may notice them and let them sit there. This also aids in becoming flexible and taking effective action. Now, let's get into some diffusion techniques. And by the way, these may sound a little bit silly at first, but they can really work. So, I encourage you to try them out and get a feel in what works for you. First, is the "Just Noticing" technique. In "Just Noticing," actually say to yourself, "I notice I'm having the thought of.." and you may use labels to describe your inner experience. Like, "there is that 'I'm unlovable thought'," or "I see you [mind] catastrophizing". Then there's the "Thanking the Mind" technique. This is where you tell your mind, "thanks for the feedback," or "thank you for this interesting thought" when having difficult thoughts. And it helps if you do so in a somewhat sarcastic manner so you don't take your thoughts too seriously. And remember that our goal here is to change our relationship with our thoughts. Next is "Mindful Watching." This is where you look at your thoughts with curiosity and openness and you kind of notice them and how they come and they go... without attempting to change or control them in any way. Finally, "Repeating a Thought." You can use a silly voice when saying the thoughts like, using the Bugs Bunny voice or talking as yoda would... "like you, I do not." Or singing your repeating it out loud over and over again until only sound remains. Basically, these are some of the defusion techniques. If you put this into practice, it might help you get some distance from your unproductive or harmful thoughts, beliefs, or emotions. So... that's it! Thank you so much for watching. If you found this helpful please don't hesitate to check out the other great information that we have at ThePsychologyGroup.com. And again, I'm Dr. Gabriela Sadurní Rodríguez and I hope you have a wonderful day!

changes in our life and being able to adapt when things change if you watched my earlier video about diffusion and if you haven't i'll put it here you know one of the best steps when we're trying to important to us oftentimes i recommend clients when they're trying to interrupt those patterns initially just pause and connect with something in the moment that could be our breath though for a lot   14. @ajmarr5671: Novel ACT Protocol from affective neuroscience

Procedure: Consistent and periodic alternation between a resting protocol (e.g. mindfulness) and the pursuit of meaningful behavior will increase motivation and positive affect (arousal and pleasure), and by making meaningful ideation more emotionally salient, will crowd out thoughts leading to anxiety and depression. This can also be denoted semantically by the conjunction of an indifference to but not avoidance of negative ideation (through the inhibition of discursive thought or ‘mind wandering’) in mindfulness with an awareness or ‘commitment’ to meaningful behavior and the values it represents, thus corresponding to ‘acceptance and commitment’ in psychotherapeutic procedure.

Explanation: Resting elicits opioid activity, or feels pleasurable, and meaningful behavior, as defined as behavior that has branching novel and positive outcomes (writing that great novel or just making the bed) elicits dopamine activity which causes arousal.  The awareness of subsequent meaningful behavior while engaging in relaxation protocols such as mindfulness elicits a ‘priming’ response, namely dopamine release that increases opioid activity, and vice versa, making meaningful behavior seem self-reinforcing or ‘autotelic’. with cognition less likely to transition to perseverative thought (worry, regret, distraction). Although mindfulness reduces discursive thought or mind wandering that can lead to negative ideation; it does not inhibit concurrent non-conscious awareness or anticipation of behavior or events subsequent to meditation that can in turn shape or ‘prime’ affective responses during a meditative session. 

A priming response, like the salivary response that precedes food or the sexual arousal that precedes intimacy, is a preparatory response that often occurs non-consciously, and changes the affective value or ‘feeling’ in the moment.  Similarly, relaxing due to ‘being in the moment’ is pleasurable, but if we were told to expect ‘bad’ news or ‘good’ news in the near future, just the awareness of future events is enough to depress or elevate our feelings, but not altering in the slightest our ‘mindful’ or relaxed state. It follows that if mindfulness is paired with the awareness of subsequent positive or meaningful behavior, then rest in mindfulness will have a greater affective tone or ‘feel better’ than if such a prospect was absent.  This is perhaps why ‘savoring’, ‘loving kindness’ meditation, and ‘flow’ experiences represent highly pleasurable and arousing experiences, as they make future positive ideation contingent to obvious or subtle pleasures (from relaxation, eating, drinking) and contrast with a lower level of pleasure during typical states of rest that generally precede a return to meaningless discursive thinking. It also explains the efficacy of popular psychotherapeutic interventions such as acceptance and commitment therapy, or ACT, that conjoins the awareness and pursuit of meaningful behavior with mindful or meditative states.
 
From ‘Galileo’s Lament and the Collapse of the Social Sciences’ a contrary and ornery take on psychology free and on the web

- Experiential Avoidance: The Most Important Idea in All of Psychology: Kind: captions Language: en This is a video on experiential avoidance, what I refer to as the most important idea in all of psychology. My name is Dr. Greg Mueller and I'm a licensed psychologist and an assistant professor living in Austin, Texas. Now, before you watch this video, please take a minute to review this disclaimer. It applies both to the content in this presentation and in future videos that I'll make. So, we're talking about experiential avoidance. And when I have this conversation with people, I very commonly show them Wikipedia because I know that this that this is something that they can review on their own. So let's take a minute and look at this. So experiential avoidance has been broadly defined as attempts to avoid thoughts, feelings, memories, physical sensations, and other internal experiences even when doing so creates harm in the long run. So the idea behind this is that as humans, we avoid as a way of coping. And very often that form of avoidance-based coping gets us into serious trouble. Now, another reason that this is so important is that a lot of what we think of as behavioral health or mental health disorders, we can think about it in terms of how avoidance plays out in the pathology of the disorder. So, let's look at several examples. So, major depressive disorder. So, people feel intense sadness, guilt, low selfworth, and they avoid through isolation or through suicide. Suicide is very often an avoidance strategy. When you talk to people that are seriously depressed, they and you ask them like, "Do you actually want to die?" Very commonly, they they say, "No, I don't want to die. I just don't want to be alive anymore." The avoidance is present in how they're experiencing the symptoms. Post-traumatic stress disorder. People have traumatic experiences. Their body becomes sensitized to threat and they have intrusive memories, anxiety, concern for their safety, and they avoid any reminders of that trauma. Their body's on alert. social anxiety, panic disorder, agorophobia, OCD, substance use disorder. Particularly, we see experiential avoidance in substance use disorder. The substance is the form of avoidance that manages the symptoms. And then there's a cycle that people get caught up in using that substance. So, several things to remember. Very often when I'm having this conversation with people about experiential avoidance, they start, you know, feeling bad like, oh, I'm doing this avoidance thing. It's it's a not so good. But it's important to recognize, you know, we're all human. We all avoid sometimes. So, examples that I commonly reference are people wear shoes so that they avoid, you know, getting their feet injured when walking around. You probably wear a coat if it's a cold day out. You have the AC on at your house to avoid the heat. And so avoidance isn't bad in and of itself, but avoidance may be a problem if it's our first solution that we jump to. I'm going to cancel all my plans with my friends. So that's an example of when experiential avoidance will get in the way of you living your life and cause functional impairment. And so it can be really tricky to try and figure out am I engaging in approach or avoidance? And so the question that I commonly pose is am I moving towards what I want or am I moving away from what it is that I'm afraid of? - What Is Behavioral Activation For Overcoming Avoidance? - Cognitive Therapy Hub: Kind: captions Language: en [Music] What is behavioral activation for overcoming avoidance? Imagine feeling stuck in a cycle where you avoid doing things because they seem overwhelming or uncomfortable. That's what avoidance behaviors are. They are actions people take to dodge unpleasant feelings, thoughts, or situations. While avoiding might give temporary relief, it often makes problems worse over time. For example, skipping social events because of fear can lead to loneliness and deepen feelings of depression. In cognitive therapy or cognitive behavioral therapy, the idea is that our thoughts, feelings, and behaviors are all connected. When someone avoids activities they once enjoyed, they miss out on positive experiences that could lift their mood. This creates a pattern where negative feelings grow stronger and avoidance becomes more ingrained. Behavioral activation is a way to break this cycle. It focuses on helping people start doing activities that are meaningful or enjoyable. The goal is to increase positive experiences and reduce avoidance. It begins with activity monitoring where you keep track of what you do each day. This helps identify patterns of avoidance and areas where you tend to withdraw. Next, you plan small, manageable activities to do each day. These can be simple things like taking a short walk, calling a friend, or doing a hobby. The key is to start with easy steps so you don't feel overwhelmed. As you get more comfortable, you gradually add more activities. This process helps rebuild your confidence and shows you that engaging in life can be rewarding. Behavioral activation is based on the idea that changing what you do can change how you feel. When you participate in positive activities, your mood often improves naturally. For example, going for a walk might reduce feelings of sadness or anxiety. It also helps challenge negative beliefs like thinking you're not capable of socializing. In practice, behavioral activation involves creating a schedule of activities that align with your interests and values. It also includes problem solving to overcome barriers, like finding ways to make activities easier or more appealing. Support from friends or family can boost motivation and help you stay on track. By consistently engaging in these activities, you start to regain a sense of control over your life. You notice that avoidance no longer dominates your days. Instead, you build a pattern of positive experiences that can lift your mood and reduce feelings of depression or anxiety. This approach is effective because it directly targets the behaviors that keep emotional difficulties going, helping you feel better step by step.

No, eso no es de lo que se trata ACT. ¿Por qué no lo aclaras? - Sí, sí, sí, absolutamente. Lo he escuchado. Y da miedo, da miedo. A veces, cuando hablas con tus pacientes sobre aceptar lo que está ahí, da miedo, ¿cierto? Especialmente si has estado sintiendo dolor, si has estado sintiendo mucha desesperanza, es realmente difícil porque les suena como: "Esto es todo. Acéptalo o déjalo, esta es tu vida". Suena a resignación. Y creo que es importante que un terapeuta de ACT enfatice que aceptación no significa que te estás rindiendo o que te estás resignando a tener una vida dictada por lo que está ocurriendo en el momento. Se trata básicamente de no controlar más la experiencia. Hacemos mucho esfuerzo tratando de controlar o evitar. Quiero sentir dolor, pero solo esta cantidad de dolor, o estoy dispuesto a sentir ansiedad, sí, pero solo esta cantidad, o solo que aparezca en esta área de mi vida. Aceptar es más como: "Muy bien, hay dolor, hay ansiedad, y no voy a tratar de evitarlo más". Y cuando enfatizamos la aceptación, creo que es importante que nuestros pacientes sepan que eso no significa que no van a trabajar duro. Recuerda que es una combinación de muchos factores que usamos en ACT. Es aceptar la experiencia que están teniendo, la ansiedad, la tristeza, y elegir comportamientos en la dirección de tus valores. Así que no eres pasivo. Es mucho trabajo, es difícil, porque tienes que comprometerte a hacer cosas en la dirección de lo que te importa. Si fuera pasivo, probablemente dirías algo como: "Muy bien, estoy ansioso. Me voy a quedar dentro, en mi casa, sin salir nunca porque estoy muy asustado". Eso no es aceptación. Aceptación es: "Estoy aterrorizada, y mi estómago está hecho un nudo, y estoy sudando, y siento que me voy a morir, y voy a dar este paso fuera de mi casa ahora mismo porque quiero ser una buena abuela y el cumpleaños de mi nieto es hoy y esto es importante para mí, y voy a dar un paso fuera de la casa". Y luego das otro, y sientes los síntomas en tu cuerpo, y aceptas que están ahí, pero no están dictando tu comportamiento. Es muy importante que hagamos esa distinción. Lo otro es que no estamos ignorando los síntomas en ACT. No estamos tratando de reducir tus síntomas. Ese no es el objetivo, pero los síntomas mejorarán cuando estés abordando otras cosas. No es eso, otra cosa que he oído, que: "Oh, solo estás ignorando la ansiedad". No estamos ignorando la ansiedad ni ningún síntoma que aparezca. Seguimos abordándolo, pero de una manera diferente. Los síntomas serán aliviados. Alguien más dijo también: "Sabes, en ACT hay mucha atención plena. Es solo atención plena". No es solo atención plena. Obviamente, estamos tratando de que la gente practique ACT. Descubrimos, redescubrimos o reconocemos nuestros valores, ¿cierto? Así que, no es solo atención plena; es la conexión de todas esas cosas diferentes lo que nos lleva a ir y vivir una vida que valga la pena básicamente. - Vamos a profundizar ahora en algunas de las estrategias prácticas para los clínicos que buscan aplicar ACT en su trabajo. Mencionaste la difusión, cambiar cómo nos relacionamos con nuestros pensamientos. ¿Puedes hablar un poco sobre esa práctica y cómo ayudas a tus pacientes a practicarla? - Sí, la difusión cognitiva puede ser una de mis favoritas, las estrategias que entran en esta categoría pueden ser de mis favoritas. Así que la difusión es, supongo, una práctica o el objetivo de lograr que nuestros pacientes reconozcan que sus pensamientos son solo pensamientos, ¿cierto? No tienen que decirte quién eres, no tienen que decirte qué puedes y qué no puedes hacer. ACT utiliza muchas metáforas diferentes, y una de ellas me viene a la mente... Ahora, escucha, tenemos que decir esto desde ya. Obviamente necesitamos el compromiso de nuestros pacientes. Nada puede ocurrir si tu paciente no está listo. Y si nuestro paciente no está listo, hay otras estrategias que podemos usar. Me viene a la mente la entrevista motivacional, muy útil cuando queremos generar una conversación sobre el cambio. Estamos asumiendo ahora que nuestro paciente está listo para empezar a hacer algo o está listo para participar en el tratamiento. Así que, cuando se trata de difusión, una de las estrategias que utilizo a menudo es imaginar que estás conduciendo un autobús y vas a, no sé, a cualquier lugar, la biblioteca. Y tienes pasajeros en tu bus, y algunos de los pasajeros son ruidosos y desagradables. Dicen cosas que dan miedo, como: "Vas a estrellar el autobús, vamos a tener un accidente. Es aterrador". Otros dicen cosas sobre ti, como: "¿Por qué hiciste eso hoy?" "Le pareces esto y lo otro a tu jefe". Ya sabes, voces que no ayudan en nada. Y sabes, todos tenemos pasajeros en nuestro autobús, y nuestro autobús puede ser nuestra mente. Y eso no significa que tengamos que detener el autobús. Seguimos queriendo ir a la biblioteca. Podemos ir a la biblioteca incluso si tenemos a esas personas ruidosas en nuestro autobús diciendo cosas sobre cómo nos sentimos o quiénes somos. Y cuando hacemos eso, ¿va a resolver todo? No, no lo hará, pero es una estrategia que en el momento puedes reconocer, ¿sabes qué? Estoy haciendo lo que me importa, aunque tengo a este pasajero ruidoso diciendo estas cosas sobre mí. Y eso es todo. Ese es el objetivo de esas estrategias. Otra que me viene a la mente y que me encanta hacer, especialmente en grupos con adolescentes, obviamente las cosas pueden salir mal, lo han hecho en el pasado, pero hay dos cosas que hacemos. Una es que elegimos una palabra que puede ser difícil, y en un grupo es un poco más difícil encontrar una palabra con la que todos estén de acuerdo. Obviamente con una persona va a ser más fácil, pero digamos que alguien dice la palabra "inútil". Y cada vez que escuchan la palabra "inútil", se sienten muy mal consigo mismos en el momento. Y digo: "De acuerdo, entonces digamos la palabra 'inútil' durante 30 segundos en voz alta, todos juntos, lo mejor que puedan. Diciendo cada sílaba lo más rápido que puedan, sin parar". Y pongo el temporizador. Y durante 30 segundos todos están diciendo: "Inútil, inútil, inútil". A los 30 segundos paramos. Siempre hay alguien que dice: "Oh, me siento peor, me siento más inútil". Está bien, las estrategias no son para todos, pero la mayoría de la gente acaba diciendo algo como: "Esa palabra perdió sentido a mitad de camino". "Me dolía la mandíbula, necesito beber agua. Me dio sed. Terminó siendo solo ruido. No tenía ningún significado". Eso es lo que quieres. - ¿Es esa la difusión? - Exacto, porque en ese momento ves la palabra como una combinación de letras y sonidos y deja de ser tan pesada, ¿verdad? Así que en ese momento, por un segundo, pudiste difuminar de esa palabra y el significado. Otra que es muy divertida, y de estas normalmente la gente se ríe, pero digo: "De acuerdo, entonces dame una frase que te desanime". Digamos que alguien quiere ir a una fiesta y realmente quiere darse a conocer. Digamos que es un chico de secundaria o alguien en el trabajo. Y es como ahora que nos estamos acercando o cuando nos acercamos a celebraciones importantes como festivos u otras celebraciones que la gente hace en eventos relacionados con el trabajo. De acuerdo, no quieres ir porque te da vergüenza porque tus colegas van a estar allí y te sientes cohibido, lo odias. Lo odias, no quieres ser criticado, no quieres llamar la atención sobre ti. Entonces, diría, en ese momento: "De acuerdo, ¿qué frase te viene a la mente que realmente te deprime?" Y lo que pasa siempre es que la gente se siente tonta, sonríen, piensan: "Oh, ¿por qué me hace mi terapeuta hacer esto? Es ridículo", pero en ese momento hubo una sonrisa, hubo una dirección, ¿verdad? Están como: "Ah, ¿por qué soy así?" Lo que digo en ese momento es: "Sal de tu carro y entra a esa fiesta. Esa es tu pausa, ¿verdad? En ese momento estás centrado, estás haciendo esa tontería, estás sonriendo, no estás prestando atención ni rumiando sobre esa frase. Sales del auto y vas y haces lo que valoras porque realmente quieres estar allí. Valoras las relaciones y simplemente estás muy asustado. Lo mismo para los adolescentes que regresan a la escuela, estas son algunas de las estrategias que puedes hacer en cualquier lugar. Y eso es lo que te permite. Te permite tener un poco de desapego de esa palabra que se siente tan pesada o de esa frase. - Eso tiene mucho sentido, y me encantan esos ejercicios. Hablemos sobre los valores. Because ACT comes from the behavior therapy tradition, ACT therapists with the collaboration of their client are going to encourage behavioral change to make the individual have opportunities to respond differently in their world perhaps to persist at chosen actions related to what’s vital and meaningful in your life or to alter how you typically respond in clinically relevant situations. Two, commitment is defined as action in the direction of what you care about even in the presence of obstacles. Acceptance and Commitment therapy has been validated mainly through correlational studies between groups that use ACT and those that don’t, or ‘between group’ designs, that unfortunately leave a lot of room for debate for the relative efficacy of alternative therapies such as CBT and other talk therapies. Here is a validation from a ‘within’ subject (individual subject) design that reduces the concepts of acceptance and commitment to clearly defined response contingencies that are precisely mapped to bio-behavioral events, or a radical behaviorism. 

A Commitment to Values works, but best while in a resting or relaxed state. Here is why.

Positivity Simplified
Persistent positive or meaningful thinking in a resting state will increase pleasure and arousal, and avoid negative ideation that elicits opposing emotional states.

Positivity Explained
Any relaxation protocol from eyes closed rest to mindfulness is pleasurable, due to the release of endogenous opioids. If concurrent persistent positive or meaningful ideation occurs (meaning is defined as thinking of or doing actions that have branching novel positive implications, or virtual positive act-outcome contingencies), this induces a feeling of arousal as mediated by dopamine systems. Dopamine and opioid systems are synergistic, or when activated simultaneously reciprocally stimulate each other, causing feelings of greater pleasure and arousal, or ecstatic states. This explains why ‘loving kindness’ meditation, savoring, peak, or flow experiences that have rest as an entailment ‘feel’ different from resting states, yet nonetheless represent unremarkable and simple neural processes that can be explained and replicated with ease by anyone.

An Aside on ACT
This procedure may be termed ‘relaxation and commitment’ in contrast to ‘acceptance and commitment’, as relaxation protocols by design incorporate the avoidance of negative ideation or an ‘acceptance’ of the status quo. The difference is that the former derives from a radical or bio-behaviorism and maps response contingencies to observable behavior, while the latter are derived from inferred cognitive processes derived from a behavior analytic theory of language.
 
A formal explanation from a neurologically based learning theory or ‘radical behaviorism’ of this technique is provided on pp. 44-51 in a little open-source book on the psychology of rest linked below.  (The flow experience is discussed on pp. 81-86.)

- Do I Need Values Before Setting Goals? ACT FAQ for Therapists: Kind: captions Language: en This is ACT FAQ, where I answer some of your frequently asked questions. So, today's question is, do values need to be established before goals in therapy? I think this question was asked because it makes sense to work out the person's values and then come up with goals based on those values. So, the goals come from those values. However, what happens if the person is really struggling to come up with their values? Coming up with values isn't easy. It can be really hard and confusing and frustrating. They might be really fused with some self-stories and thoughts about themselves that they can't get away from yet because they don't have the skills. Or they might not be able to sit with discomfort and shift straight into experiential avoidance. But, I think we can address some initial goals without values, such as, our work together can be about helping you find other ways to handle this anxiety that is showing up for you. Yes, that might not be a smart goal and it's somewhat vague and not particularly well measurable, perhaps, but it starts a dialogue of working together toward a common goal. And I agree with Russ Harris here that learning a new skill is still a behavioral goal. A new skill is a new behavior. And in the spirit of that, we aren't talking about reducing anxiety or getting rid of anxiety. We are saying, let's look at different ways of handling it when it shows up. Then, once some diffusion skills have been introduced or acceptance skills, whatever works best, then values can be revisited and more behavioral, tangible goals can be established. Remember, the Hexaflex is a dance. All the processes are interlinked with each other. So, we can move around it flexibly. It doesn't have to be done in any set order. Don't set limiting rules for yourself by thinking values must come first. Take care, make life meaningful, and goodbye.

- The 3 Brain Strategies That *Actually* Rewire Your Mind (Neuroscience Explained): Kind: captions Language: en Have you ever wondered how your brain can adapt and change throughout your life? Think of it this way: Imagine you're walking through a forest and you take the same path every day. Over time, that path becomes more defined and easier to follow. But functional imaging has advanced, and newer research has shown that our brains continue to change and adapt well into adulthood. This shift from a fixed brain to a plastic brain model has revolutionized our understanding of brain function and mental health. There are two types of neuroplasticity: structural plasticity, and this involves changes to the brain's physical structure, such as the growth of new neurons or the formation of new synapses. And then there's functional plasticity, And this refers to the brain's ability to move functions from a damaged area to other undamaged areas. Neuroplasticity gives you the power to influence your brain structure and function through your experiences and behaviors. Neuroplasticity does work both ways, so negative thinking and behaviors also reinforce certain pathways in the brain. However, once you start replacing those negative habits with positive ones, the new pathways begin to take over, helping you become more mentally strong and adaptable. To understand how neuroplasticity works, let's look at the basics of brain structure. Your brain consists of billions of neurons, which are the cells responsible for processing and transmitting information. These neurons, or nerve cells, communicate with each other through connections called synapses. When you learn something new or have a novel experience, your neurons form new connections or strengthen existing ones. And this process is called synaptic plasticity. The more you repeat an action or thought, the stronger the neural pathways become. It's like creating a well-worn path in your brain. Several key brain regions are involved in neuroplasticity: the hippocampus, which is important for memory formation and spatial orientation, which is the ability for you to be able to tell how your body's positioned in space. Then there's the amygdala, which is involved in emotional processing and fear responses. And then the prefrontal cortex, which is responsible for higher order thinking and decision making. And these areas work together to process new information, form new memories and adapt to changing environments. So that's how neuroplasticity works. Here's why It's important for building mental strength and resilience. It impacts four main areas of functioning. First, adaptability. Neuroplasticity allows your brain to adapt to new situations and challenges. And this flexibility is the basis for being able to navigate the ups and downs and develop resilience. Second is learning and memory. When you have new experiences and form new neural connections, you're able to learn new skills and retain information. Being able to learn boosts your confidence and problem- solving abilities so you can in fact, teach an old dog new tricks. The third impact of neuroplasticity is overcoming negative patterns. Neuroplasticity empowers you to change negative thought patterns and behaviors. You can consciously and intentionally create new neural pathways and up-level poor coping skills, and reshape how you respond to stress and adversity. And the fourth impact is recovery and healing. Neuroplasticity plays a vital role in recovery from brain injuries and managing mental health conditions. It offers hope for healing and improving even in challenging circumstances. Several factors can impact your brain's plasticity. There's your age. Even though neuroplasticity occurs throughout life. It tends to be more pronounced in younger brains. That said, even older adults can benefit from activities that promote plasticity. A rich, stimulating environment promotes neuroplasticity. This includes engaging in new experiences, learning new skills, and exposing yourself to diverse sensory inputs. The interplay between neuroplasticity and sensory input is one of the reasons hearing loss, vision loss and social isolation are so harmful to your mental functions. And then there's lifestyle factors. Sleep, nutrition, and exercise all play critical roles in supporting neuroplasticity. Quality sleep helps consolidate memories. A balanced diet with minimal processed foods provides nutrients for brain health. And regular exercise increases blood flow to the brain and promotes the growth of new neurons. Okay, so that's a lot on neuroplasticity. Now let's look at some practical strategies to harness the power of neuroplasticity and build mental strength. I'm going to give you three strategies. One is learning new skills. Challenging your brain with new activities stimulates the formation of new neural connections. And this could be learning something like a musical instrument, picking up a new language, or trying a new hobby. The second strategy is metacognition and mindfulness. Metacognition is thinking about thinking. It's a powerful tool for enhancing neuroplasticity and building mental strength. It involves becoming aware of your thought processes and learning to regulate them effectively. Here's how you can practice metacognition. One is self-reflection. Regularly take time to examine your thoughts and reactions. Ask yourself, "Why did I respond that way?" or, "What assumptions am I making?" Next is thought journaling. Write down your thoughts and analyze them objectively. Look for patterns or cognitive distortions. Then engage in mindful meditation. This practice helps you observe your thoughts without judgment. Increasing your metacognitive awareness. By developing metacognitive skills, you can identify and challenge unhelpful thought patterns. Improve your decision-making process. Enhance your emotion regulation and boost your learning and problem- solving abilities. Combining metacognition with mindfulness creates an effective synergy for rewiring your brain and building resilience. - How to Rewire Your Brain & Learn Faster | Dr. Michael Kilgard: Kind: captions Language: en - Welcome to the Huberman Lab podcast, where we discuss science and science-based tools for everyday life. Dr. Michael Kilgard is a professor at the University of Texas at Dallas, and he is one of the world's leading experts in neuroplasticity, which is the brain's ability to change in response to experience. Since the beginning of the field of neuroscience, meaning for well over 100 years, it was understood that the young brain can change. Kids can learn things. They can learn languages, new skills. - How to Change Your Brain & Increase Neuroplasticity at Any Age | Dr. Andrew Huberman: Kind: captions Language: en As we get into adulthood, most of our neural maps in the brain, certainly our sensory maps and our cortex, our motor maps that allow us to move in particular ways, those have been established. You can still change them, but they've mostly been established throughout childhood and into our early 20s. And if we want to modify those circuits with neuroplasticity, there are a couple of key requirements. One, you need to be alert. You can't get neuroplasticity. That is, you can't trigger neuroplasticity unless you're alert. You also have to be focused. This is critical and differentiates adult plasticity in a major way from plasticity when we're young where we can learn by passive exposure. Okay? When we're young, we can learn by passive exposure or even better by focused exposure. But when we are adults, we need alertness and we need focus. Just passively being exposed to, you know, music or to a motor pattern is not going to allow us to change our nervous system. That's been shown over and over again. Fortunately, what also has been shown over and over again is that if we are alert and we're focused and we are determined, especially if we undertake what's called incremental learning, where we go after small bits of neuroplasticity repeatedly over time, we can get as much neuroplasticity as one observes in childhood. It just takes longer and you have to do it so-called incrementally. There's a lot to say about that, but for sake of today's discussion about the vagus nerve, I just want to tell you that there's a particular pathway in the brain that involves the molecule acetylcholine. Acetylcholine is used to contract the muscles. It's released from motor neurons in the spinal cord onto muscles to contract the muscles. It's also used in the brain and elsewhere in the nervous system and it does a lot of different things. It's actually involved in generating the rhythms of the heart. But acetylcholine released from a particular nucleus in the brain called nucleus basalis. The acetylcholine released from nucleus basalis is what we call permissive for plasticity. In other words, if you have acetylcholine released from nucleus basalis into the brain, plasticity is much more likely to occur. And in fact acetylcholine released from nucleus basalis is sort of like a gate whereby if you release acetylcholine the opportunity for neuroplasticity and learning is available for some period of time. So the question therefore becomes how do you get acetylcholine released from nucleus basalis. There are these incredible experiments that have been done by Mike Merzik and colleagues showing that if you stimulate nucleusalis to release acetylcholine and you expose an animal or a human to a particular sensory stimulus, the brain remaps very fast according to that experience. Just enormous amounts of plasticity that you wouldn't observe otherwise. There are also fortunately experiments showing that if you pharmacologically increase acetylcholine that you can enhance the opportunity for neuroplasticity. You still need to do the learning. You still need to attempt to learn something. You still have to make it incremental, but the amount of plasticity is significantly increased when there's acetyloline released from nucleus basalis. So in the absence of deep brain stimulation using an electrode, which most of you fortunately will not experience because it requires drilling down through the skull and placing an electrode in basalis and assuming that you're not taking anything to increase acetyloline transmission to learn, although there are ways to do that. There are some other precursors to acetyloline or things that stimulate the release of acetylcholine such as hooperine and things like that that will open the opportunity for enhanced plasticity for a few hours. These drawbacks about nicotine are real and are critical to consider if you're going to use nicotine as a focusing agent or a so-called neutropic. Most notably, the habit forming and addicting properties, which are very robust. Now with that said, there are ways to non-farmacologically stimulate the nucleus basalis acetyloline pathway to enhance the window for plasticity and the way to do that is you guessed it through the vagus nerve. Studies in healthy humans and humans who have had for instance stroke as well as animal studies have shown that if you stimulate the vagus nerve electrically you increase the level of alertness in the brain. (Laughter) So we've done several studies - I see you can relate to that a little bit - where we wanted to put our worker rats to the test, to see if this effort-based reward training generalized to other things. So we like to expose them to new challenges, like swimming - they've been in a lab, they've never been in water. Well, the effort-based reward worker rats are more likely to dive down, like little rats scuba divers, to explore the environment. They showed more evidence of effective coping. And when we look at their brains, I think brains are gorgeous here, they show more evidence of neuroplasticity, that fertilizer, brain-derived neurotrophic factor, more complex connections with the neurons. So, we see this neuroplasticity. For the interventions and therapeutic approaches that we have currently for depression, most of those directly or indirectly increase neuroplasticity, but here we're doing it naturally. But that was with training. We wanted another way to stimulate effort-based rewards that was more spontaneous. So, we've known for a while that if you put a rat an exciting and engaging world, something called "enriched environment," kind of a Disneyland of sorts, they're busier and they have more neuroplasticity and it seems to be great for their brains. So we did this. We also look at artificial kind of manufactured stimuli, and more natural stimuli. So, we have our country rats and our city rats. They seem to be equally smart, but our country rats seem to have an edge on emotional resilience. So, they are more like those effort-based reward rats that will go out, the bold ones. And also, with our effort-based reward rats, we see lower stress hormones and higher hormones of resilience, and remember we said that was important for mental health. Interestingly, we also found that when we have a group of rats in an enriched environment and a group of rats in just a standard environment, they do things more together, not only engaging with their environment, but through cooperation. So, we've actually shown that their oxytocin that we talked about increases when they're engaged in these natural enriched environments doing things together. And that's important for our "behaviorceutical" cocktail. This doesn't surprise me, because recently in Denmark, they showed that humans - they followed about a million - who grew up in a household with more green around it, shrubs, trees, were up to 55% less likely to experience depression in their lives. If we could bottle that, that would be amazing. So, where does that leave us? We're not going to go back to the cave or to being hunters and gatherers. We're here in this advanced technologically rich world, and we benefit in many ways from that, but looking back at what we know about our ancestors and the brain, and my wise rats, I think it reminds us that we need to remember our evolutionary roots as we go forward in this world of technology and have a little bit of those effort-based rewards, especially if it's related to Nature in some way, to help us with our mental health. I had an experience where I got to put this to the test to see if an engaged enriched environment would allow the rats to show healthier brains, and I had a colleague who asked me, "Kelly, can you teach a rat to drive a car?" I thought "why would I want to do that? That's not natural." This goes against everything I thought, but we drive cars and before I knew it, we were talking about how you'd get a rat to drive a car, and how you'd shape it to go in. We decided that we'd grab the little copper bars, and of course, they would be driving to a Froot Loops tree. That's their drive-in. If you've ever wondered if you can teach a rat to drive a car, yes, you can. Not only can they drive, but they can steer, they're autocorrecting, right? This blew my mind, but more relevant for this story is when we looked at rats that were in an enriched environment versus the standard environment. The rats in the enriched environment, when we took them through the ropes of driving to see how long it would take them to learn to drive, the criterion for robust driving, they learned in 22 trials. The standard rats, we don't know how long it would take, they never really learned to drive. This blew our minds that the enriched environment made our rats better learners of technology. So, we think that our enriched rats would get their driver's license, but not so much for the rodents, they would be denied. So, as we think about our brains and what they evolved to do, the idea of taking a single pill and being able to replicate what goes on in our brains naturally seems just about as unreasonable as thinking that we could take a pill to be a better parent. You just can't do that, you have to go through the ropes. You have to have those experiences to go forward. You have to have the behavior that leads to "behaviorceuticals" to change the neurochemistry in healthy ways. So, I started with a mystery, what's going on with our brains? why are these rates increasing? And looking back and thinking about how our behavior can change not only our neurochemistry but our neuroanatomy, I think that the solution and clues may have been in our hands all along. Thank you. (Applause)

- Polyvagal Theory: What’s Supported by Science — and What’s Not?: Kind: captions Language: en I was talking to one of my mentors in the field the other day and we got into the topic of polygo theory and he gently encouraged me to look closer into some of the research as it currently stands behind poly bagel theory in an effort to keep this channel as research informed as possible. I want to share what I found with you, especially because polyagal theory and how our nervous systems work is something I talk a fair amount about in my series on stress and trauma. But what I found in my research is polyagal theory currently mixes some really important and excellent neuroscience with some interpretive claims that just go beyond current evidence. So, we'll break down some of the main claims that poly bagel theory makes that may be overstated and simplified and try to paint a fuller, more nuanced picture of how our nervous systems really work. To begin, our nervous system is fluid. It is not made of fixed states. So, polyagal theory talks about three main states. The vententral veagal where we feel calm and socially connected. the sympathetic state, often described as fight or flight, and dorsal veagal shutdown, where we freeze and immobilize. But scientists don't all agree that our nervous system actually divides into three distinct states like that. In most research, people describe patterns of parasympathetic and sympathetic activity rather than these fixed states. Because of that, we also can't think of ourselves as moving up or down these states like they're a fixed ladder. It is much more fluid than that. And different systems in our body can be active at the same time, which means can overlap. We can experience both simultaneously. For example, we might be hanging out with a friend and feel very relaxed and connected to them while feeling physically on edge in a new environment. So rather than switching between these three separate modes, our nervous system is constantly adjusting to our context in a much more fine-tuned way. And because the nervous system responses overlap and are constantly shifting, our behavior doesn't fall into one clear category either. You'll often hear in polyagal theory that each state comes with this specific way of acting, calm and social in one state, frozen or shut down in another. But when different systems can be active at the same time, our behavior just doesn't map clearly onto one single state. We can also have the exact same behavior like direct fixed eye contact that is coming from a place of confidence and openness or on the other hand maybe coming from a place of hypervigilance and anxiety. So while there are certain body language cues we can look to that sometimes signal stress or relaxation, they aren't universal. It's very culturally dependent and most the time our behavior is going to reflect a mix of activation and calm just like our nervous system itself. Third point I want to make is heart rate variability can't tell us what state we're in. While heart rate variability or HRV gives us a rough sense of how easily our bodies can adjust to changing demands like shifting between effort and rest. It is not a precise measure of safety, stress or any specific emotional state. HRV changes for many reasons, even breathing, movement, our age, overall health. So, it's telling us a lot more about our overall adaptability and the flexibility of our nervous systems rather than how we feel in a given moment. Fourth point, because the nervous system isn't a simple ladder, we don't always start with active defense or fight or flight and then shut down if that doesn't work. Sometimes we're going to freeze immediately without even trying to fight or escape in the first place. Our nervous system tends to select the protective response that feels safest for us based on a lot of factors like how much control we feel like we have, how much energy we have available, how close the threat feels, and what we've learned from past experiences. Social context and our past conditioning matter a lot because our bodies often rely on strategies that we've used to cope before. So when we're in that frozen state, coming out of it also doesn't just follow one path. There's no predictable direction of what deactivating looks like. Sometimes we may start more frozen and immobilized and move into feeling calmer and more grounded. Other times we may move from that frozen state into more fight orflight energy. So we're moving from passive to active defense. That doesn't mean our nervous systems have regulated. It just means we have more energy and mobility. That shift can be a positive sign that our capacity to act is returning. But it doesn't mean our nervous system has settled yet. Another point on the shutdown state. This state is not inherently more harmful for our bodies than fight or flight. We can't think of freezing and shutting down as more damaging to our body and our organs than fight or flight. Both shutdown and fight or flight are protective adaptive responses. And both become stressful to our bodies if they last too long without us getting to recover and rest. So what affects our health more isn't whether we fight and flight or whether we freeze. It's how chronic and unsupported our stress becomes over time. Next point on neurosception. I'd encourage you to think of neurosception more as a helpful concept than a defined brain system. So polyagal theory uses the word neurosception to describe how we subconsciously sense safety and danger. And it's true that our brains are constantly evaluating threat outside of us being aware of this. But this isn't coming from one specific biological system or piece of our anatomy. This process seems to involve a lot of different brain regions working together to interpret cues from our environment. Last point I want to make here is the evolutionary story that polyagal theory presents is more complex than it sounds. Polyagal theory sometimes describes mammals as having a uniquely social nervous system that reptiles don't have. But comparative biology shows that many non-mamal species display complex social behavior. And how our nervous systems have evolved is more gradual change over time than a sharp divide. Humans and mammals more broadly do have more complex brain networks. We have changes in how our vag nerve interacts with facial expressions and vocal tones and are more flexible in our social communication. But these features are more like refinements of older nervous systems rather than a completely new social nervous system. So after unpacking some of these claims that may be overstated or simplified, I want to end with something equally important, which is giving poly veagal theory some credit for helping highlight several ideas that are strongly supported by research. One, our nervous system really does shape how we feel and behave. One of the biggest takeaways that is very strongly supported by science is that our nervous system influences how safe or threatened we feel, how we perceive and make sense of what's happening around us, and how we respond emotionally and socially. The vag nerve also does really play an important role in regulating things like our heart rate, breathing, digestion, and our stress response. And when our nervous system is more activated or more relaxed, this deeply affects our mood, our attention, and our ability to connect with others. Second, feeling safe with others can be really deeply calming for our nervous systems. Research shows that safe social connection does help regulate stress. So those things like that warm facial expression, that gentle voice, steady eye contact really can signal safety and help our bodies settle. And humans often do regulate better together than alone if we're around people that we feel emotionally safe and supported with. Third point, fight, flight, freeze, and shutdown are real protective responses. Our nervous system has multiple ways of protecting us. It is not just fight or flight. And there are times where we move into more passive defensive responses like freezing. But even if that shutdown response in the moment makes us feel immobilized and out of control of our own body, this is an adaptive and protective way of responding to threat, not a sign of weakness. The last point I want to make is just to acknowledge that the language of poly bagel theory has helped a lot of people. Even in the places where the biology gets simplified, poly bagel theory has given us a shared language to talk about our nervous system experiences. Many people find it validating and empowering to understand their reactions through this bodybased lens and to understand again that our initial reactions are automatic and unconscious. So bringing nervous system education into therapy especially has really supported meaningful change for a lot of people and helped people judge themselves and their reactions less and find more self understanding and compassion for the very different ways that we respond to stress. So after taking this deep dive together into the science behind poly baggo theory, I hope you can approach your body and what it's telling you with even more nuance and self-standing. For me, this research has served as a helpful reminder that very often we're going to be feeling everything all at once. And even during mundane moments where there might not be much going on outside of us in our internal worlds, our experience is complex and multi-layered. Because of that, we also don't have to reach or stay in some ideal calm zen state to support healing and move out of chronic stress. It is totally okay and very common for different sensations and emotions to exist in our bodies at the same time. And even when stress is present in our bodies, it's still helpful to bring in small things that ground and support us. Learning to be curious and open towards the complexity of our inner experience leads us beautifully into the next series I'll be sharing with you all on emotional maturity. So, I'm excited to explore that more with you soon.

Being able to reduce all of the complicated interactions and unknowns of brain activity to a linear ladder sounds too good to be true, and it is. Indeed, Grossman et al. and Vertichka critique PVT as reductionist. Porges makes other assertions in his theory that current research does not back up, such as {quote} dorsal vagal shutdown, {unquote} not actually decreasing heart rate, and there being mounting evidence of complex social relationships between animals that Porges would term primitive. And finally, the experts found that Porges had shotty scholarship with half of the physiological references being inaccurately cited and others misinterpreted. Wow. Porges responded by basically saying the experts had misrepresented polyvagal theory's fundamentals, so the evidence they present doesn't apply. Porges also critiques it as a position paper by a self-selected group. Is it? Well, there don't seem to be any brow-raising conflicts of interest, but Grossman et al. also don't explain the selection process for the panel of experts, so it may be a task force of PVT haters, or it may not. Porges goes on to put the burden of proof on his critics rather than on himself, and does not address any of the shotty scholarship in his response. So, bringing the expert review and Porges' response together, Vertichka says that {quote} PVT's core assumptions are fundamentally contradicted by current physiological, neurobiological, and evolutionary data. Also, {quote} while the psychological concepts utilized by PVT, like coregulation and psychological safety, are considered valid and valuable, they predate PVT by decades and are neither clarified nor strengthened by this physiological framework that lacks empirical support." Ouch. So, what does this mean for us as mental health professionals? Well, believing in and promoting PVT to our clients can be dangerous. We, as clinicians, have an ethical and legal duty to provide the best possible care for our clients, and if we continue to use PVT knowing that it lacks evidence, then we are not providing adequate care. Clients could also misattribute serious health problems to vagus nerve activity and try treatments based in PVT that are not evidence-based and delay them getting medical help. Clients could also think, "Oh, thank goodness, this is the key to all of my trauma and attachment, and with this I can heal." When in reality, there are better treatments out there. Although, I don't know of any standard polyvagal informed treatment that is actually hazardous to clients. In fact, many of them have health benefits. I'm sure if PVT has motivated many people to attune to their bodies and take better care of themselves. It takes what could be abstract and stressful in their brain and provides them more digestible way to envision and heal that. If using PVT helps you heal, then use it. Ultimately, I do want people to heal and grow however they can. But, if you're tackling things as complex as trauma and attachment, know that PVT does not have all the answers and may even get in the way of your healing. There are better theories out there with better science and that yield better results. It's too much to get into here, but I recommend you check out the end of Dr. Veretichka's article for some suggestions. All of my sources are in the video description. Bye.

It just totally changes how you perceive your reality and reality, as we know, reality is perception. So the world starts to look really dangerous. What that means on a neurological level is that your brain starts to interpret input as really dangerous which means that sensory stimulation that shouldn't be painful will be interpreted as painful by your brain. It also really caps your performance. In life, in your body and in your life. So from an athletic standpoint, if you're dealing with these dysregulated states, you don't have as much energy available for performance, your body's not replenishing itself because when you're in these nervous system states, it's for example, in sympathetic, your body's not really focused on digesting and assimilating your food because it's much more important to get away from something that's going to kill you. Basically, if you're running away from a serial killer, it's not really important to digest your lunch. And on an ongoing basis, this can impair your digestive function, it can impair your physical recovery, but it also impairs your mental performance, your cognitive performance, your ability to connect to other people. Remember that Ventral Vagal state is social engagement. If you're in your or your Dorsal Vagal shutdown, and people are looking really threatening, how do you think you're going to relate to your partner? How do you think you're going to relate to groups of people? How do you think you're going to relate to your business colleagues, your team, right? So if everything is relationship for people, and we are relationship creatures, and then being in these stress states makes it really difficult to cultivate powerful, strong, heartfelt, authentic, for lack of a better word, relationships with people. So on every level it's affecting us, physical health, emotional health, mental health. Now I wanna be really, really clear here. This is not about changing your thoughts. This is not about changing your beliefs. There's a lot of really great programs and books and things like that around becoming aware of yourself, becoming aware of your patterns, becoming aware of what has influenced or shaped you. I think those are valuable insights but they're mostly up here. This is really physiology. Remember these branches of your nervous system are 400 million years old, They don't know language exists. You can't have a rational conversation with them. The way that we access them is through your physical body, through physical sensation, through practices that interrupt and disrupt these neural processes to bring you back to that state of social engagement. - Window of Tolerance and Emotional Regulation (Dr Dan Siegel): Kind: captions Language: en When you're coping well with the ups and downs&nbsp;of life when your thoughts are rational and&nbsp;&nbsp; your emotions are calm you are said to be&nbsp; functioning within your window of tolerance.&nbsp; The window of tolerance was originally described&nbsp;by Dr Dan Siegel as the optimal zone of arousal. If you stay within your window of tolerance&nbsp; you're able to process and successfully respond&nbsp;&nbsp; to the demands of everyday life. So let's imagine&nbsp;you get a phone call from your boss and she asks&nbsp;&nbsp; you to do additional work over the weekend now&nbsp;that stressor may increase your level of arousal,&nbsp; maybe even to put you at the edge of your&nbsp; window of tolerance but if you're still within&nbsp;&nbsp; that window you can handle the stress and stay&nbsp;clear-headed. During times of extreme stress you&nbsp;&nbsp; can move outside of your window of tolerance&nbsp; into a state of hyper arousal. The sympathetic&nbsp;&nbsp; nervous system is ignited and the fight or flight&nbsp;response activated. In this state you may feel&nbsp;&nbsp; angry, irritable, chaotic, hyper-vigilant, anxious,&nbsp;have racing thoughts and a sense of restlessness. Hyper arousal results in the deactivation of&nbsp; your prefrontal cortex which is responsible for&nbsp;&nbsp; executive function such as attention and impulse&nbsp; control. When the prefrontal cortex is essentially&nbsp;&nbsp; shut down it's very difficult to think clearly&nbsp; and rationally. Stress can also make you plummet&nbsp;&nbsp; into a hypo aroused state. The parasympathetic&nbsp;nervous system is engaged and you freeze in&nbsp;&nbsp; response to stress or danger. In this state you may feel overwhelmed, emotionally numb,&nbsp;&nbsp; exhausted, lack motivation and feel depressed. Your&nbsp; body posture may collapse or curl up in a ball and&nbsp;&nbsp; you may disconnect or dissociate in order to cope. &nbsp; So in the hypo aroused state you have essentially&nbsp;&nbsp; shut down. Everyone's window of tolerance is&nbsp; different for example Peter has a wide window&nbsp;&nbsp; of tolerance for meeting deadlines and working&nbsp; evenings and weekends. Peter can tolerate the&nbsp;&nbsp; intensity of work well and the associated emotions&nbsp; but Peter's window of tolerance quickly narrows&nbsp;&nbsp; when he's in a potential conflict situation, his&nbsp; blood begins to boil and he quickly moves into a&nbsp;&nbsp; hyper aroused state of rage. At this point Peter's&nbsp; emotions are intense and difficult to manage.&nbsp;&nbsp; We all have different windows due to factors&nbsp; such as childhood experiences, social support,&nbsp;&nbsp; coping skills and our neurobiology. For example&nbsp; trauma survivors often have narrow windows&nbsp;&nbsp; and tend to spend a lot of time in a hyper or&nbsp; hypo arousal state. Now the good news is that you&nbsp;&nbsp; can widen your window of tolerance and therefore&nbsp; increase your ability to manage stress. For example&nbsp;&nbsp; if you are hyper aroused you might find it helpful&nbsp; to use techniques that settle your mind and body&nbsp;&nbsp; such as mindful breathing, listening to calming&nbsp; music, going for a gentle walk or talking to&nbsp;&nbsp; a friend. If shifting from a hypo aroused&nbsp; state this tends to require getting more active&nbsp;&nbsp; so going for a brisk walk, doing some exercise or&nbsp; engaging socially. Stimulating the senses by smell&nbsp;&nbsp; or touch, listening to uplifting music or eating&nbsp; some food with a strong taste or crunchy texture.&nbsp;&nbsp; Psychological therapy may also widen your window&nbsp; as it can provide an external source of safety,&nbsp;&nbsp; a protected space and a personal connection&nbsp; with someone. So you can learn to modulate&nbsp;&nbsp; your internal states, to raise arousal levels when&nbsp; too low and to shift them back down when too high.&nbsp;&nbsp; So by monitoring and modulating your internal&nbsp; state you can increase resilience and promote&nbsp;&nbsp; self-regulation. I've added links to a number of&nbsp; helpful exercises in the description box below. You might also be interested in the video on the&nbsp; screen now, just click the screen to view the video.&nbsp;&nbsp; I look forward to seeing you soon with&nbsp; more mental health tools and strategies.

From a grammatical, academic, semantic and best practice standpoint, 'emotion regulation' is the more precise phrasing. The word emotion denotes what you are regulating; emotion is the object being regulated. The word 'emotional' describes the kind of regulating you are doing, you can't 'regulate' an 'emotional'.
