- Polyvagal Theory Made Simple: Kind: captions Language: en-US Polyvagal theory, developed by Dr Stephen Porges,&nbsp;reshaped our understanding of the human nervous&nbsp;&nbsp; system and the body's response to threat and&nbsp;social interactions. Before polyvagal theory,&nbsp;&nbsp; the nervous system was thought to act in a binary&nbsp;manner, like a light switch with the body's&nbsp;&nbsp; stress response being in an on or off state.&nbsp;According to this perspective, threat causes the&nbsp;&nbsp; autonomic nervous system to activate a 'fight-or-flight' response, and once the threat is gone,&nbsp;&nbsp; we return to feeling safe and calm. According&nbsp;to Dr Porges, human responses to stress are too&nbsp;&nbsp; varied and nuanced to be adequately explained by&nbsp;a binary model. Instead, he proposed a three-part&nbsp;&nbsp; hierarchy, like a ladder. At the top of the&nbsp; ladder is ventral vagal social engagement. This&nbsp;&nbsp; is a state of safety in which we can emotionally relate and connect to others. In this state we can&nbsp;&nbsp; feel more open, peaceful and curious. Moving down&nbsp;one rung we get to sympathetic activation. This is&nbsp;&nbsp; a defensive state in which the body mobilises&nbsp;us for 'fight-or-flight' in order to quickly&nbsp;&nbsp; dispatch threat. To do this, our heart beats&nbsp;faster, our breathing becomes fast and shallow,&nbsp;&nbsp; our muscles tense, and stress hormones flood our&nbsp;body. At the bottom of the ladder is dorsal vagal&nbsp;&nbsp; shutdown. When our nervous system is intensely&nbsp;activated and we still can't dispatch the threat,&nbsp;&nbsp; a protective part of the nervous system shuts&nbsp;down or freezes, like a turtle withdrawing into&nbsp;&nbsp; its shell. We may flop to the floor or curl&nbsp; up in a ball. Our heart rate, blood pressure,&nbsp;&nbsp; and facial expressions all decrease. We may&nbsp;have difficulty thinking and speaking clearly,&nbsp;&nbsp; and we can feel numb, dizzy, or disconnected. Here's a very simple example of the polyvagal&nbsp;&nbsp; ladder in action. Jane is enjoying a video call&nbsp;with an old friend. She's in a ventral vagal state&nbsp;&nbsp; and feels safe and able to connect and empathise&nbsp;with others. A loud crash upstairs startles her.&nbsp;&nbsp; Jane's sympathetic nervous system responds to&nbsp;the potential threat by mobilising her body&nbsp;&nbsp; for fight-or-flight. Jane's pupils dilate, her breathing becomes shallower and her heart beats&nbsp;&nbsp; faster. Alternatively, Jane might respond&nbsp; by entering a dorsal vagal state, a kind of&nbsp;&nbsp; "playing dead" survival mechanism of last resort.&nbsp;Jane becomes still and holds her breath. She is unable to communicate with her friend or take any&nbsp;kind of action. How Jane's nervous system will&nbsp;&nbsp; react will depend on a range of factors, not&nbsp;least her previous life experiences. Another&nbsp;&nbsp; key part of polyvagal theory is the role of the&nbsp;vagus nerve. In Latin, vagus means wandering,&nbsp;&nbsp; and true to its name, the vagus nerve wanders from&nbsp;the brain stem throughout the body, regulating&nbsp;&nbsp; many bodily functions, including heart rate,&nbsp;breathing, digestion, and immune function. The&nbsp;&nbsp; vagus nerve is responsible for the body's "rest&nbsp;and digest" response, as opposed to the "fight&nbsp;&nbsp; or flight" response of the sympathetic nervous&nbsp;system. There are two branches to the vagus nerve;&nbsp;&nbsp; ventral, meaning front, and dorsal, meaning back. A good way to understand the difference&nbsp;&nbsp; is to think of the ventral as a footbrake that&nbsp;slows you down allowing you to enter a calm and&nbsp;&nbsp; safe place, and the dorsal as an emergency brake,&nbsp;stopping you immediately in your tracks. The vagus&nbsp;&nbsp; nerve is part of the parasympathetic nervous&nbsp;system, which itself is part of the autonomic&nbsp;&nbsp; nervous system. Don't worry too much about these&nbsp;details. The key point is that the vagus nerve&nbsp;&nbsp; is separate from the sympathetic, fight-or-flight,&nbsp;pathway. The goal of the autonomic nervous system&nbsp;&nbsp; is to keep us safe and alive, and it achieves this using something called neuroception,&nbsp;&nbsp; which works a bit like an internal smoke &nbsp;detector for cues to safety and danger. Before&nbsp;&nbsp; Jane had time to think, neuroception in &nbsp;her body had already scanned her environment&nbsp;&nbsp; and used this information to make changes to&nbsp;her heart rate, breathing, and muscle tension&nbsp;&nbsp; via the vagus nerve. Neuroception takes place&nbsp;automatically and without involving the thinking&nbsp;&nbsp; part of our brain. It's the reason why you might&nbsp;feel uneasy in a situation without consciously knowing why. Neuroception is essential to survival&nbsp;as it allows us to react rapidly to potential&nbsp;&nbsp; threats and social interactions. Co-regulation&nbsp;is another core component of polyvagal theory&nbsp;&nbsp; and is fundamental to feeling safe and secure in&nbsp;relationships. The autonomic nervous system does&nbsp;&nbsp; not work in isolation and is regulated through connections with other nervous systems. These&nbsp;&nbsp; nervous systems support and influence each&nbsp;other through the mutual sending and receiving&nbsp;&nbsp; of signals for safety. Through co- regulation,&nbsp;emotional and physiological states, such as heart&nbsp;&nbsp; rate and breathing, become synchronised. When we&nbsp;feel safe and supported by others, our autonomic nervous system can manage stress and emotional&nbsp;responses better. This is why polyvagal theory&nbsp;&nbsp; is sometimes called the "science of safety." Co-regulation begins in the womb when an unborn&nbsp;&nbsp; baby hears its mother's voice, which becomes a&nbsp;comforting sound. As an infant, they associate&nbsp;&nbsp; this voice with other comforting cues, such as&nbsp;a parent's smile, and as a toddler, they learn&nbsp;&nbsp; to seek co-regulation from their parent whenever&nbsp;they feel distressed. Even when we learn to self- regulate, we continue to seek co-regulation&nbsp;so that we can feel safe, calm, and connected&nbsp;&nbsp; to others. Co-regulation can be more difficult&nbsp;for those who've experienced chronic stress or trauma as they may find it harder to establish a&nbsp;sense of safety. Faulty neuroception, that is,&nbsp;&nbsp; the inability to accurately assess whether a&nbsp;situation is safe or dangerous, can cause us to&nbsp;&nbsp; become hardwired to experience threat, stress, and&nbsp;anxiety, even when we're safe. As a consequence,&nbsp;&nbsp; we can become locked in a protective&nbsp; fight-or-flight or shutdown state,&nbsp;&nbsp; unable to connect with others. If we don't have&nbsp;a safe relationship in our life, we can get back&nbsp;&nbsp; to a ventral vagal state with safe therapeutic&nbsp;relationships and exercises that activate the&nbsp;&nbsp; vagus nerve. Even noticing micro-moments of peace&nbsp;or joy, known as glimmers, can help us to get back&nbsp;&nbsp; to a ventral vagal state faster. Like muscle&nbsp;toning, it's possible to increase vagal tone so&nbsp;&nbsp; that we can cope better with stress and return to&nbsp;a ventral vagal state faster. Here are some ways&nbsp;&nbsp; to activate and tone the vagus nerve. Breathing&nbsp;deeply and slowly from the diaphragm stimulates&nbsp;&nbsp; the vagus nerve. Techniques such as 'box&nbsp;breathing' and 'physiological sighing', that is,&nbsp;&nbsp; two inhales followed by an extended exhale, have&nbsp;been found to lower blood pressure and heart rate. The vagus nerve is connected to muscles at&nbsp;the back of the throat. Gargling contracts the&nbsp;&nbsp; muscles of the pallet, which stimulates the vagus&nbsp;nerve. Vibrations caused by singing, humming, and&nbsp;&nbsp; chanting stimulate the vagus nerve, which passes&nbsp;through the vocal chords and the inner ear, and is&nbsp;&nbsp; linked to increased heart rate variability,&nbsp; reduced illness and improved well-being. The&nbsp;&nbsp; vagus nerve is stimulated when the body is exposed&nbsp;to cold. Cold showers, splashing your face with&nbsp;&nbsp; cold water, or a blast of cold air through an&nbsp;open window dampen the fight-or-flight response&nbsp;&nbsp; and increase the rest and digest response. Vigorous movement (like walking and running),&nbsp;&nbsp; weightlifting, and somatic exercises are good&nbsp;for our cognitive faculties, gut flow, and vagal&nbsp;&nbsp; tone. Laughter induces diaphragmatic breathing,&nbsp;which stimulates the vagus nerve, lowers blood&nbsp;&nbsp; pressure, and improves mood. Body scan meditation&nbsp;can also activate the vagus nerve. Lie down and&nbsp;&nbsp; close your eyes. Starting at the top of your&nbsp;head, scan down through your body, noticing areas&nbsp;&nbsp; of discomfort. Take deep breaths and imagine&nbsp;sending relaxing energy to each part of your body. Self-havening is a technique involving&nbsp;the touch of hands, upper arms, and face.&nbsp;&nbsp; Specific motions such as cupping your cheeks or&nbsp;crossing your arms (like a self-hug) stimulate the vagus nerve. Polyvagal theory has reshaped&nbsp;our understanding of the nervous system and the&nbsp;&nbsp; way we view stress, behaviour, and well-being.   3. @LeahBensonTherapyTampa [1 likes]: PUBLIC SERVICE ANNOUNCEMENT: The Pseudoscience of Polyvagal Theory

What Your "Trauma-Informed" Therapist Might Be Getting Wrong About Your Nervous System.

First: This is not about WhEtHeR POlyVAgAL "WoRkS" or not. It is about its "scientific" underpinnings.

Polyvagal Theory (PVT) is marketed as the "science of safety," used to explain everything from social anxiety to chronic trauma. 

However,  predictive processing and a landmark 2026 consensus paper led by Paul Grossman and 38 world-leading physiology experts make it clear. There is a massive computational and "biological gap" between PVT marketing and current cognitive and evolutionary science.

1. The "Vagal Myth" of Evolution
PVT claims the human nervous system evolved in three distinct, hierarchical stages (the "Vagal Ladder"). Science says otherwise.

The Anatomy is Wrong: PVT teaches that the "old" dorsal vagus only causes freezing/fainting and the "new" ventral vagus creates social connection. In reality, both pathways are ancient, work together, and exist in nearly all mammals.

The "Ladder" is a Lie: Evolution does not work like a ladder where "higher" levels override "lower" ones. Your nervous system is an integrated web, not a tiered cake.

Respiratory Sinus Arrhythmia (RSA): PVT uses RSA as a "pure" measure of the ventral vagus. Scientific consensus proves that RSA is heavily influenced by breathing rate and depth, making it an unreliable metric for "emotional safety" when used in isolation.

2. The Hazard of "Biological Essentialism"
The danger of PVT is that it reduces complex human experiences to oversimplified—and often incorrect—biological "states."
Pathologizing Physiology: By labeling certain states (like "Dorsal Vagal Shutdown") as "primitive" or "bad," therapists can inadvertently make patients feel like their bodies are broken or "evolutionarily stuck."

Ignoring the Mind: PVT suggests that you can "hack" your way to mental health through purely physical cues. This ignores the role of narrative, culture, and cognitive appraisal in how we actually feel.

Clinical Oversimplification: Therapists may focus on "toning the vagus" while missing the actual psychological or systemic issues causing a patient's distress.

3. Why This is "Bad Science"
In a rigorous clinical setting, data must lead the theory. In Polyvagal Theory, the theory often ignores the data.

The "Just-So" Story: PVT acts as an explanation that sounds plausible but lacks empirical proof. The 2026 consensus highlights that there is zero evidence for many of PVT’s core claims regarding the specific "social engagement system."

The Placebo of Certainty: PVT provides a sense of certainty by using "sciency" terms, which can act as a powerful placebo. 

However, basing treatment on a false map of the body can lead to a dead end when complex symptoms don't resolve through simple "vagal exercises."

​4. Predictive Processing: Why the Brain is Not a Passive Switch.
​Polyvagal Theory relies on a Reactive Model of the brain: an external stimulus happens, and your vagus nerve "switches" you into a specific state. Predictive processing flips this on its head, proving that the nervous system is proactive, not just reactive.
​
Top-Down Construction: In the PP framework, your brain isn't just "receiving" safety or danger signals from the vagus nerve. Instead, the brain is constantly generating predictions about what is happening in the body based on past experience, context, and expectations. Your "state" is a best-guess construction, not a mechanical response to a nerve impulse.
​
The Error of Interoception: PVT suggests that "Dorsal Vagal" states are biological facts. Predictive processing shows that these states are actually interoceptive inferences. If your brain predicts that a situation is inescapable, it will down-regulate your system. The "shutdown" isn't caused by a "primitive" nerve; it is a sophisticated, high-level calculation made by the brain to conserve energy.
​
Context Over Anatomy: PP explains why two people can have the exact same physiological "vagal tone" but feel completely different emotions. One might feel "calm" while another feels "bored" or "depressed." PVT ignores context dependency, whereas Predictive Processing proves that your beliefs and environment determine the "meaning" of your physical sensations.

THE REALITY CHECK FOR PATIENTS
You have the right to Scientific Transparency. 
Your nervous system is a sophisticated, integrated masterpiece—not a series of primitive switches. Demand that your therapist respect the actual complexity of your biology.

- Cognitive Fusion and Defusion in ACT (Acceptance & Commitment Therapy): Kind: captions Language: en-US There's a type of mindfulness-based therapy&nbsp; called Acceptance and Commitment Therapy,&nbsp;&nbsp; and an important concept in&nbsp; Acceptance and Commitment Therapy&nbsp;&nbsp; is the idea of cognitive fusion and defusion. Cognitive fusion describes those times when we're&nbsp;&nbsp; so tightly stuck to our thoughts that we become&nbsp; fused with them. We can't separate ourselves&nbsp;&nbsp; from our thoughts, and so our thoughts become our&nbsp; reality. And when we're in a state of cognitive&nbsp;&nbsp; fusion, we can feel removed from the world&nbsp; outside our thoughts, and from what we're doing,&nbsp;&nbsp; and from the people around us, and it can be hard&nbsp; to pay attention to anything outside our head. &nbsp; The opposite of cognitive fusion is cognitive&nbsp; defusion. Cognitive diffusion involves taking&nbsp;&nbsp; a step back from what's going on inside our minds&nbsp; and detaching ourselves from our thoughts. In this&nbsp;&nbsp; state of diffusion, we can observe our thoughts&nbsp; without getting caught up in or lost in them,&nbsp;&nbsp; and we can just allow them in and accept them&nbsp; and let them be and let go of them if we want. One way we can practice cognitive diffusion&nbsp; is to label your thoughts. Anytime you notice&nbsp;&nbsp; that you're starting to be fused with your&nbsp; thoughts, you can simply take a step back&nbsp;&nbsp; from your thoughts by labeling them as thinking,&nbsp; or daydreaming, or worrying, or ruminating, or&nbsp;&nbsp; planning. Just labeling whatever type of thought&nbsp; you're having with a one or two-word description,&nbsp;&nbsp; and doing this helps you take a step back from&nbsp; the thought and focus less on the content of&nbsp;&nbsp; your thought and more on just the fact that&nbsp; you're thinking, or worrying, or day dreaming,&nbsp;&nbsp; or whatever the nature of your thought is.&nbsp; And this makes it less likely that you'll&nbsp;&nbsp; get sucked in by those thoughts, or carried&nbsp; away by them, or become fused with them. Or you can say to yourself, "I'm just&nbsp; thinking, just worrying." And putting&nbsp;&nbsp; the qualifier "just" in front of the thought&nbsp; helps take away some of the power of that&nbsp;&nbsp; thought and makes it easier to let go. Or you can label the content of your thought&nbsp;&nbsp; as being just a thought. So if you're thinking, "I&nbsp; can't do anything right," you can reframe this as,&nbsp;&nbsp; "I'm just having the thought I can't do&nbsp; anything right." Or if you're thinking,&nbsp;&nbsp; "This is going to be terrible," you can reframe&nbsp; that as, "I'm just having the thought that this&nbsp;&nbsp; is going to be terrible." Instead of "Nothing&nbsp; ever goes my way," "I'm just having the thought&nbsp;&nbsp; that nothing ever goes my way." And by prefacing&nbsp; our thoughts with the disclaimer that this is&nbsp;&nbsp; just a thought, we reinforce the idea that&nbsp; our thoughts are not facts. And every time&nbsp;&nbsp; we remind ourselves of this, we take away some&nbsp; of the power that our thoughts have over us. And if you're still having trouble letting go of&nbsp; your thoughts, you can imagine yourself writing&nbsp;&nbsp; down each thought on a balloon and then&nbsp; releasing that balloon up into the air and&nbsp;&nbsp; just allowing that thought to float from&nbsp; your mind as the balloon floats away. Now, sometimes instead of just letting go of&nbsp; our thoughts, it can be helpful to look at the&nbsp;&nbsp; content of our thoughts and just get a sense of&nbsp; how accurate or how biased that thought may be,&nbsp;&nbsp; and see if there may be a different way&nbsp; of looking at things and thinking about&nbsp;&nbsp; them that's more helpful to you, which is&nbsp; something we'll explore in the next video&nbsp;&nbsp; about reframing your thoughts and cognitive&nbsp; restructuring. And if you'd like to check&nbsp;&nbsp; out my online mindfulness-based stress&nbsp; reduction and cognitive therapy program&nbsp;&nbsp; where these videos come from for free,&nbsp; you'll find a link in the description. And&nbsp;&nbsp; please hit the like button and subscribe&nbsp; to my channel for more videos like this.

- Trauma-Informed Care Explained: Safety, Trust & Nervous System Regulation | Dr. Arielle Schwartz: Kind: captions Language: en Let's go into [music] the topic of traumainformed care from a resilienceinformed lens. I'd love to start us out with the principles of traumainformed care and you can find these online at the cdc.gov. The first of these is safety. Of course, we want our people to feel safe with us and what facilitates basic safety in the therapeutic relationship is trustworthiness and transparency. I mentioned earlier in this module that safety is um a tricky word sometimes because it can sometimes point out where we're not safe and currently not safe. And we live in a world where a lot of the people that are coming to us for support are currently in unsafe experiences. Whether that's relationally, whether that's culturally, whether that's due to access to resources such as a house, such as financial resources. And so the relative safety within the therapeutic environment is the foundation of good care. And then on top of that, also being able to attend to those safety factors outside of our work. Sometimes we need to collaborate with other community services to work on housing support or access to food and so forth in order to also support that safety. As I mentioned, trustworthiness and transparency facilitates that safety in the room. And that another key element here is having access not just on that dependency between client and you as the only source of support, but also building in more peer support systems. Whether that's attending support groups, whether that's finding who are the good support people in our clients lives outside of therapy, who can they call when they're struggling, who's a safe person to talk about um their difficulties with or to bring their emotional vulnerability to. Within therapy, we also look at the importance of collaboration and mutuality. We've already been speaking about this, haven't we? Collaboration is the ability to kind of co-pilot the process together to ensure that your client can tell you what's working and what's not working and so that we feel like we're on an even playing field as we progress through treatment together. We want our clients to feel empowered and at choice at every stage of the treatment process. And then the final principle here is that we are acknowledging and respecting the cultural, historical and gender issues that may be impacting our clients sense of self and sense of safety in the world. So the phasic model of trauma treatment has been and continues to be the most wellressearched evidence-based supported approach to successful trauma recovery. And for many many years, I want to say for about 30 years, starting in with Judith Herman's first book in the early 1990s, I think it was 1992 that she first came out with her book trauma and recovery and introduced the phase-based model. It was always referred to as the triphasic model. Three phases of treatment. The first of which is to establish stability and safety by developing resources. Then we go into phase two where we process traumatic material in a well-paced and regulated manner. And phase three where we reintegrate new experiences into our sense of identity and our relationships. But just this year, which is 2023 to locate when I'm uh teaching this material, Judith Herman came out with her bookend book. If you think of trauma and recovery as the beginning of her career, she came out with a follow-up book that is called Truth and Repair. And she introduces a fourth phase to trauma treatment, which is justice, reparations, the recognition of the impact of what has happened and seeking rehabilitation for offenders. Now, it's important here to distinguish that it's not always about punishment of offenders. In fact, most trauma survivors have enough sensitivity that even though there's a part of them that may be rageful and hateful and and carry fury towards their perpetrators, ultimately what they want is reparations and rehabilitation. So as we look at this phasic model to trauma care, we can think of our trauma treatment as occurring in an arc and that perhaps we move across these phases in within the entire arc of our entire of our whole treatment process which can be over many years. But we can also recognize that inside of a single session, we can also move through smaller arcs where we're developing some stability and a sense of safety in the here and now that lets us do a little bit of a deepening in to some of the trauma related material. And then we have a new gem. We have an understanding of self and we integrate that into our overall sense of identity and we bring that into our relationships. And that can happen in these smaller arcs perhaps even dipping into what justice looks like, what reparations would look like, even if they cannot get that from the external systems which may not be doing the work of trauma recovery that the individual is doing. But how could they give that to themselves now? Or seek smaller, safer spaces where justice is recognized, where that dignity and respect for what they've been through is honored and attended to. Few of my favorite perspectives on the trauma-informed practice. First of all, trauma-informed practice prioritizes our clients complexity, the social context, and the therapeutic relationship throughout all phases of treatment, including the assessment phase, the diagnostic phase, and the treatment process. And the first requirement is to adopt an approach which will retain our patients or our clients in therapy long enough for the therapist and patient to form a shared understanding of what is happening and to find a way of working together. Here's the truth. When we don't have enough safety and trustworthiness and collaboration in our work with our people, they do not stay in therapy. And that's the biggest cost of therapy that's not well delivered is that people leave and then maybe they don't ever go back to therapy because they didn't have a good experience. So we need to work with all of this in mind so that we really create a safe environment so that we can support our people to heal. I refer to this as a foundation of safety that you know we might have a whole list of questions that we might ask someone about their past as we gather information and we try to understand who they are and how they've become who they are and what symptoms they might have. But before we go into gathering all of that information about the past, we need a foundation of safety. And we achieve this by orienting clients to the here and now and inviting them to pay attention to the cues of safety in the room and reminding them that there's plenty of time for our work together. I mentioned earlier that I used to work in community mental health and that can be a tricky setting to achieve this. First of all, when we were trained to do our um assessments, we were trained to do this simultaneously typing into a computer our intake sessions. So, someone would come in, we've never met each other, we have a whole list of questions we need to get through in an hour or 90 minutes, and we're typing their answers into the computer. It does not lend itself well to a foundation of safety. we aren't that able to track what might be happening or the impact of these questions on the other person and it disrupts the social engagement and the attachment relationship between you and the client periodically as you keep turning towards a keyboard and a computer. So being very mindful that sometimes our systems are set up in in a manner that isn't as traumainformed as it needs to be. And so we have to then advocate for things like um I might not get a diagnosis at the be at the end of an intake. In fact, it might take closer to a month or several months because my client feels overwhelmed when I ask a lot of questions about their symptoms. And um and I don't want to um discourage them from staying in treatment. I'll share one brief story here. I had a woman that came to me after reading the the complex PTSD workbook and she really related to that book and she came to see me to and told me a story about the first time she went to go see a therapist and it was in a community setting. The therapist very similar to what I was describing was asking a whole list of questions and at some point the therapist asked a question. client has no memory of what that question was, but she ran from the room and she ended up standing next to her car in the parking lot and she had no memory of how she got there and it was terrifying. So, we are really wanting to track how is the person tolerating the process at each stage uh along the way so that we're not overwhelming them. That tolerance of the affect and the sensation we we often address through looking at this window of tolerance. This was developed by Dan Seagull and it's been adapted by others to refer to as the window of capacity. What is our capacity to respond effectively to emotions and sensations? And we think of the window of tolerance as this optimal zone of nervous system arousal. And when we're above that zone, when we're out of the window at the top, we're in hyperarousal, irritability, restlessness, panic, anxiety. And when we're below that window of tolerance, we're in hypoarousal, right? And that we can drop into states of collapse, helplessness, hopelessness, despair, depression. And this also recognizes that those high arousal states, they they're not meant to be sustained. We're not meant to be in our sympathetic nervous system for days or weeks or years on end. And that ultimately our nervous system will counterbalance that by taking us down into the parasympathetic. And when we speak about polyagal theory, we'll illuminate this a whole lot more because we'll see why we can drop into these nervous system states that are characterized by this hypoarousal parasympathetic but shut down and collapse. When we're initially in our phase one um borrowing from Judith Herman, our phase one treatment, we are trying to establish safety and stability. And we do this by learning how to be in the window, right? We create these well-paced therapeutic interventions that are helping our clients work through the traumatic memories without becoming overwhelmed or shutting down in the process. So, we start with this focus on regulation and staying inside of the window. Once we have some of that safety and stability in place, we can move into our phase 2 work where we're working the edge of the window of tolerance, helping clients to successfully handle a wider range of affect and sensations. As we're doing our history taking with our people, I just want to remind us again that there's little clinical value in focusing on a list of questions when this interferes with the relationship. So, I invite you to use questions to facilitate conversations in a well-paced manner that helps you learn about your client's lives. A clinical interview then is also going to be offered at a pace that's not overwhelming the client so they don't end up in the parking lot, right? We don't want to rush the process because that can impair their willingness to continue. Clients may not be able to talk about their distresses as symptoms, right? We might be asking questions and they're going, "Well, I don't know if I do that or this is just simply who I am." So, we really need to be savvy and listen to what's not being said, watching the body language, tracking that window of tolerance, and sometimes even educating the clients that that they can help us pace the process by them noticing how they're doing all along the way. This is especially true when we are working with individuals with dissociative symptoms and when we're developing a case conceptualization. In other words, a case conceptualization is a big picture of who is this person? How do we understand them in the context of their social, cultural, developmental experiences in life? How has this shaped them? That case conceptualization can sometimes be accomplished in a 90-minute intake session and sometimes it can take months. When we're building our capacity to work with our clients and help to do this safely, there's a skill that I want to make sure that you have in your toolbox. And it's a skill that I initially learned when I was trained in EMDR therapy in 2001, and I've used this ever since. And it's really about the recognition that we need to be at choice about when we're going to think about the hard stuff. And what trauma does is it really interferes with that sense of choice because trauma is not something that we choose and it also interrupts that sense of choice that we have about when to think about traumatic experiences. So suddenly we're thinking about the traumatic events in the middle of the night or when we're trying to parent our children and those kinds of experiences. And so to reclaim a sense of choice is the first step in recovery. And it's important to know that you get to be a choice about whether or not this is a good time to think about any distressing memories from the past. And you get to make an agreement with yourself that you will only focus on traumatic memories when you feel supported and resourced. So you can have this conversation with your clients and they'll get it. They're like, "Oh, okay. I really do need to build this." I often think of if you're going to go to the gym and strengthen any muscle, we're strengthening the capacity for containment and choice through repeated practice.

And we can bring ourselves back to our earlier example of Pavlovian conditioning, because many studies have been done both in animals and in humans showing that, for instance, if you pair a tone, a bell or a buzzer with a foot shock that an animal or a person will brace themselves for the foot shock. Eventually you can just give the bell or a tone and the person will experience that same freezing up or the same fight or flight or freeze response. So you conditioned that. But eventually what happens is the tone... The bell no longer evokes that response, okay? So you see this as a reversal of the classical conditioning and we call that reversal extinction. So the retelling of this traumatic or fearful narrative, excuse me, fearful narrative is essentially an extinction process. Now, how is this done? One can do this in a therapist office face-to-face, that's sometimes done. It's sometimes done in group type settings where people actually stand up or sit in front of a group small or large and recount in detail their traumatic experience.
